unit.name: Theme: Life and Death
unit.subtitle: The origin of the universe, the sanctity of life, abortion, euthanasia and beliefs about the afterlife.

lessons.title: The Origin of the Universe and Stewardship
lessons.description: Creation accounts across six religions and Humanism; dominion, stewardship and environmental responsibility.
lessons.content_html:
Framing the Question

One of the oldest questions asked by human beings is: where did the universe come from? Modern science offers the Big Bang theory as an evidence-based account. Religious traditions offer creation narratives, theological frameworks and ethical duties derived from understanding the world as God’s creation. These two types of account are not always in conflict — but the relationship between them is complex and contested. This lesson examines how six world religions and a non-religious worldview approach the origin of the universe and what that means for how human beings should treat the natural world.

Christianity

The Bible opens with two accounts of creation in Genesis. Genesis 1 presents a structured, six-day creation in which God creates light, sky, land, vegetation, animals and finally humanity. On the sixth day, God creates human beings in the imago Dei (image of God): the text affirms that both male and female are created in God’s image. At the close of creation, God declares it “very good” (Genesis 1:31). Genesis 2 offers a more intimate account in which God forms the man from the dust of the ground.

Christian beliefs about stewardship derive from Genesis 1:28 (God instructs humanity to “have dominion” over the earth) and Psalm 8:6 (God has made humanity “ruler over the works of your hands”). While “dominion” was once interpreted as licence to exploit, contemporary Christian environmental theology increasingly emphasises stewardship — caring for creation on God’s behalf. Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) is a landmark document in this tradition, calling for an “ecological conversion” and insisting that care for the poor and care for the environment are inseparable. Christian Aid works to address global poverty and climate justice, drawing on the principle of global citizenship.

Key Fact

Genesis 1:28 gives humans “dominion” over creation; Psalm 8:6 affirms human responsibility over “the works of your hands.” Pope Francis’s Laudato Si’ (2015) develops a theology of environmental stewardship, arguing that care for creation is a moral and spiritual obligation for all Christians.

Judaism

Jewish beliefs about the origin of the universe are grounded in Genesis 1 and 2, which Orthodox Jews understand as divine revelation, while Reform Jews may interpret the text more allegorically. The concept of tikkun olam (repairing the world) gives Jewish environmental responsibility a theological basis: the world is broken and humans are called to work with God to restore it. The related principle of bal tashchit (do not destroy) prohibits unnecessary waste or destruction of natural resources.

Tu B’Shevat (the “New Year of the Trees”) is an ancient ecological awareness day celebrated by planting trees and eating fruit. The Talmud records the story of Honi who, on seeing an old man planting a carob tree that would take seventy years to fruit, was told: “just as others planted for me, so I plant for those who come after me.” Maimonides’ thirteen principles of faith (principle 10 — God’s knowledge of human actions) also supports the idea that human treatment of the world is morally accountable before God.

Islam

In Islamic teaching, Allah created the universe: the Qur’an describes this in multiple passages, including Qur’an 36:81 which speaks of Allah’s power to create and recreate. The concept of fitra (natural disposition or inner nature) teaches that human beings are created in a state of innate recognition of God and moral awareness. The concept of khalifah (stewardship / trusteeship) is central to Islamic environmental theology: human beings are not owners of the earth but trustees, accountable to Allah for how they treat it (Qur’an 7:54 affirms Allah as the creator and establisher of order in the natural world). Muslim environmental organisations draw on these principles to advocate for sustainability and climate justice.

Hinduism

Hindu views of the origin of the universe are diverse. The Rig Veda (10:129) presents a “Hymn of Creation” that is philosophically agnostic: it wonders whether even the gods know how creation began. The Bhagavad Gita (11:7) offers a vision of the universe as the cosmic body of Vishnu, all things contained within the divine. The universe is not a one-time creation but cycles through vast periods of creation, maintenance and dissolution (srishti, sthiti, pralaya). Hindu teaching on stewardship draws on the principle of ahimsa (non-harming) applied to the environment: many Hindus regard rivers, forests and mountains as sacred and deserving of protection. The Bhagavata Purana teaches that harm to the environment is harm to God’s creation.

Sikhism

The Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mool Mantar (page 1), affirming God as the one creator (Ik Onkar — One God). Sikhs believe the universe was created by God, although unlike Judaism or Christianity, Sikhism does not have a detailed creation narrative. Stewardship teaching is drawn from several passages in the Guru Granth Sahib (pages 21 and 1037), which affirm that the natural world is God’s gift and must be respected and cared for. The concept of sewa (selfless service) extends to environmental action: serving the world that God has created is a spiritual act. Khalsa Aid, the Sikh international relief charity, puts these principles into practice in disaster relief and environmental projects.

Key Fact

Sikhism has no detailed creation narrative, but the Mool Mantar (Guru Granth Sahib 1) affirms Ik Onkar — God as one creator. Environmental stewardship draws on Guru Granth Sahib pages 21 and 1037. Sewa (selfless service) extends to care for the natural world as service to God.

Buddhism

Buddhism is unique among the traditions studied here in having neither a creation story nor a creator God. The universe is understood as arising through dependent origination (paticca-samuppāda in Pali): all phenomena arise in dependence on conditions and pass away when those conditions cease. Buddhist environmental ethics flows from the first precept (not harming) and from Right Action (part of the Eightfold Path): harming the environment harms sentient beings, which violates both the precept and the path. The Lam Rim Buddhist Centre, a well-established British retreat centre, is actively engaged in environmental sustainability projects as an expression of these values.

Non-Religious and Humanist Views

Non-religious thinkers and Humanists accept the scientific account of the universe’s origin. The Big Bang theory, developed in the twentieth century, holds that the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state that expanded and cooled over time. Stephen Hawking explored how the laws of physics themselves may explain the origin of the universe without requiring a creator. Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection explains the diversity of life without design or purpose. Richard Dawkins argues for “blind evolution” — that the process of natural selection operates without intention or goal. Humanist Climate Action advocates for environmental responsibility on the basis of human flourishing and the wellbeing of future generations, without reference to any religious obligation.

Some believers see an irreconcilable conflict: if the Big Bang and evolution explain origins, there is no need for a creator. Dawkins takes this view. However, many religious thinkers argue that science and religion answer different kinds of question — science asks ‘how?’ and religion asks ‘why?’ Pope John Paul II, in his 1996 message to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on evolution (paragraphs 3 and 4), affirmed that evolutionary science and Catholic faith are compatible, provided that the spiritual dimension of the human person is not reduced to biology alone. Many religious scientists hold both commitments simultaneously: the Big Bang describes the mechanism; God’s creative act is the reason behind the mechanism.

Dominion theology emphasises human authority over creation; it can be used to justify the exploitation of natural resources. Stewardship theology emphasises responsible care: humans are managers, not owners, and will be held accountable for how they treat what has been entrusted to them. The shift from dominion to stewardship language in Christian environmental theology reflects both theological development and the urgency of the contemporary climate crisis.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers a large topic — for ‘Explain two beliefs’ questions, focus on giving two distinct religious traditions with one source of authority each. Don’t just describe what each religion says; explain why it matters — for example, why the concept of khalifah leads Muslims to environmental responsibility, or why tikkun olam gives Jews a particular motivation for environmental action. For 15-mark evaluations, always include a non-religious perspective (Humanist Climate Action, Hawking, Dawkins) alongside at least two religious views, and reach a justified conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All six world religions affirm that the universe has a divine origin, though their accounts differ significantly — from Genesis 1 (Christianity/Judaism) to Ik Onkar (Sikhism) to paticca-samuppada without a creator (Buddhism). Humanists accept the Big Bang and evolution as the scientific account of origins.
  • Christian stewardship draws on Genesis 1:28 and Psalm 8:6, developed in Laudato Si’ (2015). Jewish tikkun olam and bal tashchit, Islamic khalifah, Hindu ahimsa, Sikh sewa and Buddhist paticca-samuppada all ground environmental responsibility in their own theological frameworks.
  • The debate between dominion and stewardship within Christianity, and between religious and non-religious approaches to environmental ethics, is a key evaluative axis for this theme.

practice_questions.text:
'Science has made religious accounts of creation unnecessary.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Big Bang theory (Hawking) provides a scientific account of cosmic origins without requiring a creator.
• Darwin's evolution by natural selection explains the diversity of life without design or purpose.
• Dawkins argues that 'blind evolution' shows the appearance of design in nature can be explained entirely naturalistically.
• Humanist Climate Action draws on environmental ethics without requiring a religious framework.
Arguments against:
• Many believers argue science and religion answer different questions — science asks 'how?', religion asks 'why?' — so they cannot make each other unnecessary.
• Pope John Paul II (1996) affirmed that evolution and Catholic faith are compatible, showing religious thinkers engage seriously with science rather than ignoring it.
• Religious stewardship frameworks (khalifah, tikkun olam, Laudato Si') provide moral motivations for environmental action that science alone does not provide.
• Buddhist paticca-samuppada is consistent with scientific accounts of dependent causation — Buddhism never claimed a creator God to be displaced.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides, multiple sources, non-religious view, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

The scientific theory that the universe originated approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state that expanded rapidly — the dominant scientific account of cosmic origins.
The understanding that human beings are given authority over creation and may use it for human benefit — derived from Genesis 1:28 ('have dominion').
The theological position that human beings are responsible for caring for God's creation on God's behalf, as managers rather than owners.

lessons.title: The Sanctity of Life, Abortion and Euthanasia
lessons.description: Six religions respond to abortion and euthanasia; sanctity vs quality of life in debate.
lessons.content_html:
The Value of Human Life: A Universal Question

When does human life begin? When, if ever, is it acceptable to end it? In the UK, abortion has been legal (under certain conditions) since 1967, and the debate about assisted dying continues in Parliament. Most major religions take a position on both questions, ranging from absolute prohibition to qualified permission.

The central tension runs between two principles. The sanctity of life argument holds that human life has an intrinsic, inviolable worth that cannot be forfeited by circumstance. Against this stands the quality of life argument: that what matters is not merely biological existence but whether life is experienced as meaningful and free from excessive suffering.

Key Fact

The sanctity of life holds that every human life has intrinsic, God-given worth from conception to natural death. The quality of life view holds that what matters is whether life contains sufficient wellbeing and freedom from suffering to be worth living. These two principles underpin every religious and non-religious argument on abortion and euthanasia.

Legal and Human Rights Context

On euthanasia, the Dignity in Dying campaign argues that individuals should have the right to end their own suffering. The ‘Right to Choose’ framing in the abortion debate likewise centres on personal autonomy over a religious conception of sanctity. Both campaigns reflect a wider shift in how the state and public discourse frame bodily autonomy.

The Abortion Act 1967 made abortion legal in Great Britain (not Northern Ireland, where different legislation applied until 2019) up to 24 weeks of pregnancy, provided two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy would involve a greater risk to the woman’s physical or mental health, or to any existing children, than terminating it. After 24 weeks, abortion is permitted only in exceptional circumstances — for example, where continuing the pregnancy would endanger the woman’s life or where there is a serious foetal abnormality. The 24-week threshold roughly corresponds with the point of foetal viability outside the womb, though this point has shifted as neonatal medicine has advanced. The law does not frame abortion as a right but as a permitted medical procedure under defined conditions — a distinction that both pro-choice and pro-life campaigners continue to contest.

Christianity and Catholicism

Christianity teaches that human beings are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27 — imago Dei). Genesis 1:31 records God declaring all he had made ‘very good’, and Jeremiah 1:5 describes God knowing the prophet before his formation in the womb — both verses are read as affirming the value of life from its earliest stages.

The Catholic Church takes the most explicit position. The Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 2270, states that human life must be respected and protected from the moment of conception. On euthanasia, Evangelium Vitae (Pope John Paul II, 1995), paragraph 65, teaches that the direct and voluntary killing of an innocent person is gravely wrong, even to relieve suffering. The Church supports palliative care and the Sacrament of the Sick for the dying. Some other Christian denominations have expressed qualified openness to assisted dying in limited circumstances.

Key Fact

Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 2270 states: “Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.” This makes abortion morally impermissible for Catholics regardless of circumstances. Evangelium Vitae (1995), paragraph 65, extends the same absolute prohibition to euthanasia, describing it as a “grave violation of the law of God.”

Judaism

Jewish law (halakha) centres on pikuach nefesh — preserving life overrides almost all other commandments, including Shabbat (Talmud Bavli Yoma 84b). The Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches that whoever destroys a single soul destroys an entire world; whoever saves one saves an entire world.

On abortion, the Mishnah Oholot 7:6 rules that where the mother’s life is endangered the foetus’s life may be sacrificed to save hers — the foetus is not a full legal person. Most Orthodox authorities permit abortion only to save the mother; many Conservative and Reform rabbis permit it more broadly. Judaism does not share the Catholic absolute prohibition. On euthanasia, the tradition overwhelmingly forbids actively hastening death, though there is more flexibility on withdrawing treatment that merely prolongs dying.

Judaism is not a monolithic tradition, and different movements apply halakha with differing degrees of strictness. Orthodox Judaism generally holds that abortion is prohibited except where the mother’s life is in genuine danger — the foetus has sanctity but does not yet hold the full legal status of a person (nefesh). Conservative Judaism tends to permit abortion in a somewhat wider range of cases, including serious foetal abnormalities or severe risk to the mother’s mental health. Reform Judaism places considerable weight on the woman’s autonomy and wellbeing, and generally supports her right to make the decision in consultation with her rabbi and healthcare providers. Across all branches, the view that the foetus is a potential life deserving serious moral consideration — not a mere clump of cells — is shared; the disagreement is about how much that potential life’s weight can be overridden by other considerations. In exam answers, this internal diversity is a strength: it shows you understand that “Judaism teaches X” is always a simplification.

Islam

Islam teaches that human life is a trust (amanah) from Allah and that only Allah has the right to give or take life. The Qur’an (5:32) teaches that to save one life is as if to save all of humanity; Qur’an 6:151 commands: do not kill your children.

Most Islamic scholars regard abortion as forbidden (haram) after ensoulment — when Allah breathes a soul into the foetus (Qur’an 32:9). Different schools debate when ensoulment occurs, but abortion after this point is regarded as very grave; some scholars permit it in very limited circumstances before that point. Most Islamic authorities forbid euthanasia, seeing it as usurping Allah’s sovereignty over life and death.

Hinduism

Hindu teaching sees all life as sacred because it contains atman — the universal soul. The Bhagavad Gita (2:17) teaches that the eternal soul is indestructible, passing through many lives (samsāra); killing interrupts a soul’s journey, not merely a biological life.

The principle of ahimsa (non-violence, Yajur Veda 40–43) leads most Hindu authorities to oppose abortion and euthanasia, as both involve deliberate harm to a being containing atman. There is no single central authority issuing binding rulings, and in practice attitudes vary widely; the question of whether withdrawing futile treatment differs morally from active killing is debated.

Sikhism

Sikhs believe human life is a precious gift from God — an opportunity to draw closer to the divine and escape samsāra. The soul in all living beings is universal (Guru Granth Sahib 441), and Sikh Gurus explicitly condemned female infanticide. Sikh teaching generally discourages abortion, regarding it as interference with God-given natural processes, though many Sikhs weigh individual circumstances. On euthanasia, the consensus is that hastening death is wrong, though withdrawing futile treatment that merely prolongs dying is more permissible.

Buddhism

Buddhism’s first of the Five Precepts is to refrain from taking life. Both abortion and euthanasia involve the intentional ending of life, violating the Precept and creating negative kamma. Buddhist teaching is not absolutist, however: the Dalai Lama has suggested that karuṇā (compassion) — working with dukkha rather than simply prolonging it — may make euthanasia an act of compassion in some circumstances. Theravāda teaching is generally against abortion, since conception marks the start of a new life in the rebirth cycle, but there is no central institution issuing binding rulings and positions vary.

Non-Religious Views

Peter Singer’s concept of speciesism challenges the automatic special status of human life: what matters morally, he argues, is an organism’s capacity for conscious experience, not its species. A foetus at an early stage may therefore have less moral status than a developed non-human animal. Dignity in Dying and similar campaigns use a situationist approach: rather than applying an absolute rule, they ask what is best for this particular person in these circumstances.

Humanists argue that the emphasis should be on ‘life before death’ — improving the quality of the life that is lived. On abortion, many Humanists support a woman’s right to choose. On euthanasia, they support the right of individuals facing terminal suffering to choose the timing and manner of their death, seeing this as an expression of human dignity and self-determination.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 15-mark evaluation question on sanctity of life topics, the most common failure is giving only one side. You need at least one argument for the statement, at least one against, and a clear personal conclusion. Use precise sources: Catechism 2270 (Catholic on abortion), pikuach nefesh / Talmud Yoma 84b (Jewish priority of life), Qur’an 5:32 (Islamic sanctity), and Peter Singer’s speciesism (non-religious challenge). Remember: Dignity in Dying and ‘Right to Choose’ are the named non-religious organisations on this topic. Spelling, punctuation and grammar count for 5% of the 15-mark question — write in continuous prose, not bullet points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The sanctity of life holds that human life has intrinsic worth from God; the quality of life view holds that what matters is the experience of life, not biological existence alone. Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism all uphold the sanctity of life but differ in detail on abortion and euthanasia.
  • Key sources to deploy: Genesis 1:31 and Jeremiah 1:5 (Christian); Catechism 2270 and Evangelium Vitae 65 (Catholic); pikuach nefesh / Talmud Yoma 84b and Mishnah Oholot 7:6 (Jewish); Qur’an 5:32 and 6:151 (Islamic); Bhagavad Gita 2:17 and ahimsa / Yajur Veda 40–43 (Hindu); Five Precepts / kamma (Buddhist).
  • Non-religious views (Dignity in Dying, Right to Choose, Peter Singer’s speciesism) challenge religious positions by centring autonomy and quality of experience over doctrinal rules about sanctity. Engaging with both sides and reaching a justified conclusion is essential for Mastering-level answers.

practice_questions.text: Give two religious reasons why a believer might oppose euthanasia.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each of two correctly grounded reasons from: God gives and takes life (any religion) / human life is made in God's image (Christianity) / pikuach nefesh — preserving life is a supreme duty (Judaism) / life is a trust from Allah, only He can take it (Islam) / first Precept — do not take life (Buddhism) / ahimsa — non-violence (Hinduism / Sikhism). Must be a religious reason, not a general objection.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the 'sanctity of life'?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Human life has intrinsic, God-given worth and must be protected at every stage from conception to natural death. Secure: Human life is sacred and must be protected. Developing: Life is important to religion. Emerging: Confused or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe Jewish beliefs about the value of human life, including beliefs about abortion.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains pikuach nefesh and Talmud Yoma 84b; explains Mishnah Oholot 7:6 on the mother's life taking priority; shows awareness of the diversity between Orthodox and Reform views; notes the Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 'save a world' teaching. Secure: Two or more elements with at least one source. Developing: General statement that 'Judaism values life' without specific sources or nuance. Emerging: Simple statement with no religious grounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Buddhist teaching on ahimsa and kamma shapes Buddhist attitudes towards euthanasia.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the first Precept (do not take life); explains kamma (intentional acts of killing create negative kamma); acknowledges the Dalai Lama's view on karuna and working with dukkha; explains why this means Buddhist attitudes are not absolutely uniform. Secure: First Precept and kamma correctly explained and linked to euthanasia. Developing: General reference to Buddhism opposing killing without specific teachings. Emerging: Vague claim that 'Buddhists don't agree with it'.

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting views on abortion — one religious and one non-religious.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Religious view fully developed with source (e.g. Catholic: Catechism 2270, imago Dei, life from conception; or Islamic: Qur'an 6:151, ensoulment via Qur'an 32:9, only Allah has sovereignty over life). Non-religious view fully developed (e.g. Peter Singer's speciesism — capacity for conscious experience matters more than species; or Humanist autonomy — the woman's right to choose). Each view clearly explained and distinct. Secure: Both views correctly identified with some use of sources. Developing: One view well explained; the second underdeveloped. Emerging: Vague reference to 'for and against'.

practice_questions.text: 'Religious believers should always oppose both abortion and euthanasia.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues that many traditions do oppose both (Catholic absolute prohibition; Islamic sovereignty of Allah; Buddhist first Precept), citing specific sources for each. Then argues that the picture is more nuanced: Jewish law permits abortion to save the mother; some Buddhist scholars allow euthanasia as compassion; even Christian denominations differ. Non-religious challenge: Dignity in Dying and Peter Singer. Clear, justified personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed; some sources used; conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing. Emerging: Simple opinion with no engagement with evidence.

lessons.title: Beliefs about Death and the Afterlife
lessons.description: Heaven, hell, resurrection, purgatory, akhirah, samsara, mukti and Humanist views on death across all six religions.
lessons.content_html:
What Happens After Death?

Every religious tradition has developed teachings about what happens after physical death. These beliefs shape how adherents understand the purpose of earthly life, how they treat the dying, how they mourn and how they think about justice in a world where wrongdoing often appears to go unpunished. Humanists, by contrast, hold that death is the end of personal existence. This lesson examines beliefs about death and the afterlife across six religious traditions and a non-religious worldview, following the canonical order: Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Non-religious.

Christianity

Christians believe in life after death grounded in the resurrection of Jesus. The New Testament affirms that Jesus rose from the dead and that this promises resurrection for all believers. Jesus tells Martha in John 11:24–27: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die.” Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:42–44) describes the resurrection body as imperishable, glorious and spiritual, in contrast to the physical body that is perishable and weak.

Christian beliefs about the afterlife include heaven (eternal life with God), hell (separation from God) and, in Catholic theology, purgatory (a state of purification after death for souls not yet ready for heaven). The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1020–1023) describes the particular judgement each person faces at death and the final vision of God in heaven. Catechism 1030 addresses purgatory and 1033 affirms the possibility of damnation for those who permanently reject God’s love. Protestant denominations generally reject purgatory, holding that the believer passes directly from death to the presence of God.

Key Fact

Christian afterlife beliefs: heaven (eternal life with God), hell (eternal separation from God), purgatory (Catholic: state of purification). Scripture: John 11:24–27 (resurrection promise); 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 (nature of the resurrection body). Catholic teaching: CCC 1020–1023 (judgement and heaven); CCC 1030 (purgatory); CCC 1033 (damnation).

Judaism

Jewish beliefs about the afterlife are more diverse than Christian ones, and in many strands of Judaism this life takes priority over speculation about the next. The Hebrew Bible contains the concept of sheol — a shadowy, undifferentiated realm of the dead rather than a place of reward or punishment. Later Jewish thought, especially in the period of the Second Temple, developed concepts of resurrection, judgement and olam ha-ba (the world to come).

Orthodox Jews affirm bodily resurrection and divine judgement; Reform Jews tend to understand olam ha-ba more metaphorically or focus on legacy and the memory of the righteous. Jewish funerary practice (see the lesson on funeral rites) reflects these beliefs — burial rather than cremation is traditional, expressing the hope of resurrection.

Islam

The Islamic concept of the afterlife is called akhirah. Islam teaches that after death, the soul enters a state of waiting (Barzakh) until the Day of Judgement. On that day, all people will be raised and judged by Allah according to their deeds and faith. The Qur’an teaches that Allah has the power to resurrect the dead: Qur’an 46:33 affirms that the One who created the heavens and the earth is not unable to resurrect the dead. Qur’an 3:16 speaks of those who pray for forgiveness and protection from the punishment of the fire — affirming both the reality of hell (Jahannam) and the hope of paradise (Jannah).

Islamic funeral practice is closely connected to the belief in akhirah: the body is washed and shrouded, buried promptly and placed facing Makkah. The speed and simplicity of Islamic burial reflect the belief that the body should be returned to the earth from which it was created, ready for resurrection.

Hinduism

Hindu beliefs about death centre on the cycle of samsara (the cycle of birth, death and rebirth). The Bhagavad Gita (2:12–13) teaches that the atman (the eternal self or soul) is never truly destroyed: just as a person changes clothes, the soul moves from one body to another at death. The ultimate goal is moksha — liberation from the cycle of rebirth and union with Brahman (the ultimate reality). The path to moksha may take many lifetimes. Karma (the moral law of cause and effect) determines the conditions of each reincarnation.

Sikhism

Sikh beliefs about death are closely related to Hindu ideas but with a distinctive theological emphasis. Like Hindus, Sikhs believe in samsara (the cycle of rebirth) and karma. The soul’s goal is mukti — liberation from the cycle of rebirth and union with Waheguru (God). The Guru Granth Sahib (page 13) affirms that the soul that truly meditates on God’s name achieves liberation. In Sikhism, mukti comes not through ritual or caste but through God’s grace (nadar), devotion (bhakti) and righteous living. Death is not feared but understood as the soul’s return to its source.

Key Fact

Sikh afterlife belief: samsara (cycle of rebirth driven by karma), with mukti (liberation and union with Waheguru) as the goal. Guru Granth Sahib 13 affirms that meditating on God’s name leads to liberation. Mukti is achieved through God’s grace, devotion and righteous living — not through caste or ritual.

Buddhism

Buddhist afterlife teaching is distinctive because of the teaching of anatta (no fixed self). If there is no permanent self, what is it that is “reborn”? Buddhists explain this through the analogy of a flame passed from candle to candle: something is transmitted, but it is not the same flame, nor a completely different one. What carries forward is kamma (the Pali term for the moral force of intentional actions) and the mental formations (sankhāras) that arise from it — not an unchanging soul.

The goal of Buddhist practice is nibbāna — the complete cessation of the cycle of rebirth, achieved when kamma is exhausted and craving is extinguished. The Triratna tradition includes members who interpret rebirth not as literal life-to-life reincarnation but as moment-to-moment arising and passing away of experience — a more psychological reading of the doctrine.

All three traditions — Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism — teach some form of samsara (the cycle of rebirth). However, they differ in what is reborn. Hinduism affirms the atman (eternal, unchanging soul) as what transmigrates. Sikhism also affirms the soul’s journey across lives toward God. Buddhism denies a permanent soul (anatta) — what transmigrates is a stream of kamma and consciousness, not an unchanging entity. The goals also differ: Hinduism seeks moksha (union with Brahman), Sikhism seeks mukti (union with Waheguru), Buddhism seeks nibbāna (cessation of rebirth through extinguishing of craving).

Non-Religious and Humanist Views

Humanists understand death as the end of personal existence. There is no afterlife, no soul that survives the body, no resurrection or reincarnation. The Humanist tradition emphasises making the most of the one life we have and finding meaning in relationships, achievements, contribution to society and the legacy we leave behind. Grief is real and important; Humanist funeral ceremonies mark the significance of the life that has ended without religious language. The emphasis is on “life before death” rather than consolation from promises of an afterlife.

Believers often argue that afterlife teaching provides motivation for ethical living: if actions have consequences beyond this life (judgement, karma, kamma), people have reason to live well even when no human authority can see them. Critics argue the opposite: that focus on the next life can devalue this life and that the Humanist emphasis on “life before death” provides a stronger motivation to improve the world now. This is a productive axis for evaluation in extended-response questions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For this lesson, learn both the specific scriptural references and the theological terms: John 11:24–27 and 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 for Christianity; CCC 1020–1023 (judgement), 1030 (purgatory), 1033 (damnation); Qur’an 46:33 and 3:16 for Islam; Bhagavad Gita 2:12–13 for Hinduism; Guru Granth Sahib 13 for Sikhism. For 15-mark evaluations, structure your answer as: agree (with sources), disagree (with sources, including a Humanist view), justified conclusion. Never use bullet points in extended-response answers — use full paragraphs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christianity: heaven, hell and (Catholic) purgatory — grounded in John 11:24–27 and 1 Corinthians 15:42–44. Judaism: sheol (early), olam ha-ba (the world to come) and resurrection. Islam: akhirah, Barzakh (waiting), Day of Judgement, Jannah and Jahannam (Qur’an 46:33, 3:16).
  • Hinduism: atman transmigrates through samsara toward moksha (Bhagavad Gita 2:12–13). Sikhism: soul journeys through samsara toward mukti by God’s grace (Guru Granth Sahib 13). Buddhism: kamma and consciousness transmigrate without a fixed soul, aiming for nibbāna.
  • Humanists believe death is the end of personal existence — the emphasis is on ‘life before death’. Beliefs about the afterlife shape funeral practices, ethical motivation and attitudes toward the dying across all traditions.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in an afterlife is essential to living a good life.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Islamic teaching of akhirah (Day of Judgement) provides direct motivation for ethical living — actions have eternal consequences (Qur'an 46:33).
• Hindu karma and samsara mean that how one lives this life determines the conditions of future lives — belief in rebirth incentivises moral behaviour.
• Christian belief in heaven and hell (CCC 1033) provides a framework of ultimate justice: wrongdoers cannot escape divine judgement.
• Sikh mukti — achievable through devotion and righteous living — gives the ethical life a cosmic significance beyond mere social approval.
Arguments against:
• Humanists live ethically without any afterlife belief — moral behaviour is grounded in empathy, reason and care for others in this life alone.
• Buddhist Triratna tradition shows that afterlife beliefs can be interpreted psychologically (moment-to-moment rebirth) without undermining the ethical commitments of the Five Precepts.
• Jesus's teaching in the Gospels includes living ethically for the sake of the Kingdom of God, not merely to avoid hell.
• Secular psychological research shows that ethical behaviour is shaped primarily by environment, relationships and social norms — not by theological beliefs about the afterlife.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides sustained, multiple traditions referenced, Humanist view included, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

lessons.title: Funeral Rites and Evaluating Life and Death
lessons.description: How religious and Humanist funeral rites reflect beliefs about death; evaluation skills for the theme.
lessons.content_html:
Funerals as Belief Made Visible

A funeral is not merely a social custom — it is theology made visible. The way a community treats the body of the dead, the words spoken at the graveside, the choice of burial or cremation, the prayers offered or withheld: all of these express what the community believes about what happens after death. This lesson examines how different traditions conduct funerals and why, and then develops the evaluation skills needed for extended-response questions on the Life and Death theme.

Christian Funerals

Christian funerals reflect the belief in resurrection and the hope of eternal life. The service typically includes prayers, hymns, a sermon and scripture readings affirming resurrection — often John 11:25 (“I am the resurrection and the life”) or 1 Corinthians 15. The body may be buried or cremated: burial has historically been preferred because it follows the pattern of Jesus’s own burial and reflects the hope of bodily resurrection, but cremation is now widely accepted across most Protestant denominations.

Catholic funerals are especially shaped by the Catechism. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1684–1690) describes the Order of Christian Funerals as a rite that commends the dead to God, proclaims the resurrection, offers consolation to the bereaved and expresses the solidarity of the whole Church. The Mass of the Resurrection (Requiem Mass) may be celebrated. Prayers for the dead and for the purification of their souls in purgatory are a specifically Catholic element; Protestant services do not include such prayers because most Protestant traditions reject purgatory.

Key Fact

The Catholic Order of Christian Funerals (CCC 1684–1690) commends the dead to God, proclaims resurrection and offers consolation. Catholic funerals may include the Requiem Mass and prayers for the dead (linked to purgatory); Protestant funerals typically do not, reflecting theological differences about the afterlife.

Jewish Funerals

Jewish funeral practice emphasises speed (burial usually within 24 hours of death, or as soon as possible), simplicity and equality. The body is ritually washed (tahara) and dressed in plain white shrouds (tachrichim) — the same for rich and poor, expressing the equality of all before God. Burial is traditional (not cremation), reflecting the Orthodox belief in bodily resurrection. The Kaddish prayer is recited by mourners — not as a prayer for the dead but as an affirmation of God’s greatness even in grief.

After burial, the bereaved enter a period of intense mourning called shiva (seven days), during which family members stay at home, are visited by friends and community members, and are relieved of everyday responsibilities so they can grieve fully. Shiva reflects the Jewish emphasis on community support and the sanctity of grief.

Muslim Funerals

Islamic funerals reflect the beliefs in akhirah (the afterlife) and the resurrection. Burial must be prompt (usually within 24 hours). The body is ritually washed and wrapped in a simple white shroud (kafan), and the Janaza (funeral prayer) is performed before burial. The body is placed in the grave without a coffin (where local law permits) and positioned facing the direction of Makkah (qiblah).

The direction of Muslim graves reflects the belief that at the resurrection, the dead will rise facing Makkah. In some British settings, a shroud-only burial without a coffin may not always be possible due to legal requirements, and local Muslim communities navigate this sensitively. The simplicity and speed of Islamic burial reflect tawadu (humility before Allah) and the belief that the body belongs to God and should be returned to the earth promptly.

Hindu Funerals

Hindu funerals are typically cremation ceremonies, reflecting the belief that the atman (soul) is released from the physical body at death and continues its journey through samsara. The body is seen as a temporary container; burning it assists the soul’s departure. The cremation is usually performed by the eldest son, who lights the funeral pyre or activates the cremation. Prayers and mantras from the scriptures (including the Bhagavad Gita) are recited. A period of mourning follows, often thirteen days in traditional practice. The ashes are often scattered in a sacred river (such as the Ganges), or in Britain into a river or the sea.

Sikh Funerals

Sikh funeral practice (Antam Sanskar, “last rites”) also centres on cremation, reflecting the belief that the body is a temporary garment for the soul and that cremation releases the soul to continue its journey toward mukti. The Kirtan Sohila (the night prayer from the Guru Granth Sahib) is recited at the cremation. Readings and singing of hymns (shabads) from the Guru Granth Sahib accompany the ceremony. The ashes are typically immersed in a river or the sea. Grief is acknowledged but Sikhs are encouraged to trust in God’s will (hukam).

Buddhist Funerals

Buddhist funeral practice varies considerably between Theravāda and Mahāyāna traditions, and between cultures. Cremation is predominant (reflecting the teaching of anicca — impermanence — and the example of the Buddha, whose remains were cremated). Monks or community members recite suttas (Buddhist scriptures), meditate and transfer merit to the deceased. In Theravāda tradition, transfer of merit involves dedicating the positive kamma generated by good deeds to the deceased, who may then accept this to improve their rebirth conditions. Funeral ceremonies are occasions for reflection on anicca (impermanence) and the urgency of the dhamma path.

Humanist Funerals

Humanist funerals celebrate the life of the person who has died, without religious language or reference to an afterlife. A trained Humanist celebrant works with the family to create a personalised ceremony that reflects the individual’s life, values and character. Music chosen by the deceased or family, personal tributes, poetry and readings from secular literature may all be included. The ceremony acknowledges grief honestly and affirms that the person’s significance lies in the memory they leave and the difference they made in others’ lives. Humanist funerals are now one of the most common forms of non-religious funeral in Britain.

Key Fact

Burial is traditional in Christianity (following Jesus’s pattern; hope of bodily resurrection), Judaism (Orthodox: bodily resurrection; equality of all in death) and Islam (body returned to earth, facing Makkah for resurrection). Cremation is traditional in Hinduism (soul released from body to continue samsara), Sikhism (body as temporary garment; soul released toward mukti) and Buddhism (reflects anicca; follows the Buddha’s example).

Evaluation Skills: Constructing a Balanced Argument

The 15-mark evaluation question requires you to argue on both sides and reach a justified conclusion. A common mistake is to present one side powerfully and then dismiss the other side in a sentence — this limits your marks. Both sides must be developed with evidence. Here is the structure that scores highest:

Step 1: Agree paragraph — Give at least two reasons why someone could agree with the statement. Include at least one named source of religious authority (scripture, catechism paragraph, a named scholar from the spec). Explain what the source says and why it supports the statement.

Step 2: Disagree paragraph — Give at least two reasons why someone could disagree. Include at least one different source of religious authority, AND at least one non-religious view (Humanist, Atheist, or a secular philosopher named in the spec such as Peter Singer).

Step 3: Justified conclusion — Don’t just summarise. Take a position: state which side you find more convincing and explain specifically why. The conclusion should follow logically from your argument — not introduce new evidence at the last moment.

Common mistakes to avoid: Using bullet points (this prevents you from developing arguments and blocks evaluation marks). Writing only about one religion when the question covers the theme (you must include multiple traditions where the spec allows). Dropping in a named source (e.g. “the Bible says…”) without explaining what it says or why it supports your point.

To score at the highest level, you must weigh the evidence — not just list it. Weighing means explaining why one argument is more or less convincing than another. For example: “While the Catholic Catechism (1020–1023) provides a detailed framework for what happens after death, a Humanist would argue that these claims are unprovable and that focusing on life before death is more practically useful for guiding human behaviour.” This shows that you understand both positions and can assess their relative strengths.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on funeral rites, always link the practice to the belief: “Muslims bury the body facing Makkah because at the resurrection the dead will rise facing the direction of prayer” is a developed point; “Muslims bury the body facing Makkah” is not. For 15-mark evaluations on this theme, remember the spec requires you to include non-religious views — Humanist funerals, Peter Singer’s ‘speciesism’ on the sanctity of life, or Humanist Climate Action on the environment. Never use bullet points in extended responses: always full paragraphs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Funerals make belief visible: burial (Christianity, Judaism, Islam) reflects hopes of resurrection or the body’s return to earth; cremation (Hinduism, Sikhism, Buddhism) reflects beliefs in the soul’s release or impermanence. Catholic funerals may include Requiem Mass and prayers for the dead (CCC 1684–1690); Humanist funerals celebrate the individual life without religious language.
  • Jewish shiva (seven-day mourning) and Islamic kafan (shrouding) and qiblah (grave direction) are distinctive practices reflecting each tradition’s theological framework. All traditions share the function of communal support for the bereaved.
  • For 15-mark evaluation: structure as agree (with sources) → disagree (with sources and a non-religious view) → justified conclusion. Weigh evidence, avoid bullet points, and ensure your conclusion follows from your argument rather than simply restating both sides.

Developing: One point developed.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two contrasting practices (e.g. Islamic burial — kafan, qiblah, speed — rooted in belief in resurrection of the body and akhirah (Qur'an 46:33); Buddhist cremation — reflecting anicca, the example of the Buddha, transfer of merit to the deceased) each developed with a source of authority and explanation of why the practice flows from the belief.
Secure: Two contrasting views, one source, some development.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious funeral rites are more meaningful than Humanist funerals.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Catholic funerals connect the bereaved to centuries of tradition, scripture (John 11:25) and the community of the Church (CCC 1684-1690) — this communal dimension adds significance beyond the individual.
• Religious funerals affirm resurrection or rebirth, giving mourners hope that death is not the final word.
• Islamic, Jewish and Sikh funeral rites are precise and purposeful — each element (kafan, shiva, Kirtan Sohila) carries theological weight that a purely secular ceremony may lack.
Arguments against:
• Humanist funerals are personally tailored to the individual's life, values and character — supporters argue this is more genuinely meaningful than following a set liturgy.
• For the non-religious bereaved, a religious funeral may feel alien or dishonest — a Humanist ceremony may better reflect the reality of the person's life and beliefs.
• The purpose of a funeral is to comfort the bereaved and honour the dead — Humanist ceremonies achieve this without requiring shared theological commitments.
• Research on funeral satisfaction consistently finds that personalisation is the factor most linked to mourners feeling the ceremony was meaningful.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides sustained, multiple religious traditions referenced, Humanist view included, clear justified conclusion that weighs the evidence.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

glossary_terms.definition: The Catholic funeral liturgy — a set of rites including the Reception of the Body, the Liturgy of the Word, the Liturgy of the Eucharist, and the Rite of Committal — that commend the deceased to God and comfort the living.
The Jewish seven-day period of intense mourning following a funeral, during which the bereaved stay at home, receive visitors, and are supported by the community.
The white cloth in which a Muslim body is wrapped before burial, symbolising equality and the purity of the soul before Allah.
In Sikh teaching, liberation from the cycle of samsara and union with Waheguru (God) — the ultimate goal of the Sikh soul.
A non-religious funeral ceremony conducted by a trained celebrant, celebrating the life of the person who has died without reference to God, the afterlife or religious ritual.
